steps.title: National rules
steps.body: Spain's law sets minimum ageing for reds. Crianza: 24 months, at least 6 in oak. Reserva: 36 months, at least 12 in oak. Gran Reserva: 60 months, at least 18 in oak. Joven, young, has little or no oak. These terms appear on the back label, often with a seal.

steps.title: Rioja's rules
steps.body: Rioja sets stricter oak rules. Crianza needs at least 12 months in barrel. Reserva needs 12 months in barrel and 36 months in total. Gran Reserva needs 24 months in barrel and 60 months in total. Tempranillo's thick skins and moderate tannins suit long oak ageing, which softens it and adds vanilla, spice and leather.

steps.prompt: Order the Rioja categories by minimum ageing.
steps.explanation: Each step demands more time in barrel and bottle.

steps.title: Time and taste
steps.body: Long ageing changes Tempranillo: fruit shifts from fresh red cherry to dried fig and prune, colour fades from ruby to garnet and brick, and tertiary notes of leather, tobacco, mushroom and cedar appear. Traditional Gran Reservas, from producers like López de Heredia, can be drunk 30 years later.
steps.highlight: From fresh fruit to leather and tobacco

steps.prompt: How long must a Rioja Gran Reserva spend in barrel at minimum?
steps.explanation: 24 months in barrel, within 60 months of total ageing.

steps.title: What you learned
points: Spain's law sets Crianza, Reserva and Gran Reserva ageing
Rioja requires longer barrel ageing than the national minimum
Ageing turns Tempranillo's fruit into leather and tobacco
